title: UK to provide Ukraine with long-range drones as part of £260m package
description: In a statement released ahead of the latest meeting of the group of 36 countries committed to supporting Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire or peace
body: In a statement released ahead of the latest meeting of the group of 36 countries committed to supporting Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire or peace agreement - the government said the UK is also building maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to help Ukraine's war effort.Burnham, who is co-chairing the meeting, said the UK must do everything it can to make sure Ukraine can defend itself from Russian attacks throughout the winter.The prime minister said: "Plunging millions of Ukrainians into the freezing cold and starving them of heat and warmth won't see Putin win this war, it will only cement our resolve to support Ukraine."That is why I am determined the UK will do everything we can to ensure Ukraine is able to defend itself from Russia's barrage of attacks and systematic striking of critical national infrastructure."Before this latest support package was announced, government figures put the amount of support provided by the UK for Ukraine since Russia invaded the country in February 2022 at £35.5bn., externalIn recent days, Ukraine has struck oil refineries in southern Russia, and has repeatedly hit the Crimean Bridge - a significant logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.Meanwhile, Russian forces have been focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before winter with attacks on critical infrastructure.The UK is among a number of countries also supplying Ukraine with lightweight missiles which are being used to intercept Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine's strike rate is now close to 70%, more than double what it was just a couple of months ago, Downing Street said.The UK also pledged further air defence support this week and sanctioned Russia's 10 major oil producers.Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the government was delivering on a promise for more support for Ukraine at the Budget."Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes," he said.Meanwhile, on Friday Burnham will head to Brussels for a UK-EU summit, where both sides hope to unveil new agreements on food, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime.

schema.headline: UK to provide Ukraine with long-range drones as part of £260m package

title: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history
description: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a
body: It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment. "In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.Four other owners then had the painting.The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

schema.headline: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history

title: Parents live in fear paedophile nursery worker harmed their children
description: Parents are calling for mandatory CCTV in nurseries after a worker who looked after their children was later exposed as a paedophile.Nathan Bennett wa
body: Parents are calling for mandatory CCTV in nurseries after a worker who looked after their children was later exposed as a paedophile.Nathan Bennett was jailed in February for multiple counts of sexual abuse, including two counts of rape, against five boys at Partou King Street nursery in Bristol. His crimes were discovered after a CCTV review.Bennett previously worked as an apprentice for 18 months at another nursery in the Somerset area - which the BBC is not naming – which does not have CCTV.A number of parents whose children went there said they lived in fear about what could have happened to them at the nursery. The government said a panel was examining the use of CCTV in nurseries.Warning: This story contains distressing detailsBennett's victims at Partou King Street nursery were two and three years old at the time of his offences. In February 2025, concerns were raised over his behaviour with the children, specifically a group of five who the prosecution said he would "favour".He was suspended from the nursery after CCTV of him putting his hands down a boy's trousers was reviewed.There is no evidence he committed any offences while he worked at the Somerset nursery, or that there were safeguarding failures there. Avon and Somerset Police said it had not identified grounds to warrant a criminal investigation at the site.Det Insp Lucy Forde, who led the investigation into Bennett's crimes, previously told the BBC she feared only a fraction of his crimes could be proven."He's worked in childcare and has had access to children for a number of years," she said."My worry is there will be other victims that we haven't been able to identify, that are too young to understand what's happened to them," Forde added.After learning of Bennett's offending, a number of parents whose children went to the Somerset nursery shared their worries about what could have taken place. The BBC has changed their names to protect their children's identities.Rachel, whose children attended the nursery, said she became suspicious of Bennett after witnessing him being overly tactile with her child in her opinion.The BBC has seen messages from the time exchanged between Rachel and her partner, in which concerns about Bennett's behaviour were discussed, describing him as "weird".They discussed raising concerns about him and eventually complained to management about their son being repeatedly left in soiled nappies and being sore.Rachel said they eventually asked for their child to be moved away from Bennett's care."My son was always on Nathan's lap - there would be times where I would see him stroking him on his arm, kissing him on the forehead or cheek," she said."There was something inside me that knew straight away that's not right," she added.Rachel said she saw Bennett taking her child into the nappy changing area alone with the door closed on one occasion."I came to pick up my son and I could hear him crying - the changing room door was closed so I waited for a while."Nathan came out with him, alone, and said 'I'm not sure what's up with him, he never seems to like his nappy being changed','" she said.Rachel said healthcare professionals had since referred her child for an assessment by specialists who deal with cases of sexual assault.If you have been affected by this story or would like support then you can find organisations that offer help and information at the BBC Action Line.James, whose children attended the nursery at the same time, said he witnessed Bennett being "too physical" with children."Most times I went to pick up my children he was holding a child on his lap or making physical contact with a child," he said."More often than not, the child looked like they were trying to get away, but he was holding them there. I didn't see other nursery staff with children on their lap," James said.He said he verbally complained to nursery managers about Bennett."I told them I had observed Nathan being physical with children – in my opinion too physical."Their response was 'isn't it great how cuddly he is?'," he said.Bessie Martin, a former colleague of Bennett's at Partou King Street nursery in Bristol, previously told the BBC she had also witnessed him holding children on his lap."I would see a child try to wriggle away or stand up and walk off, but he'd say 'sit here and we're going to read a book'," she said.She became a whistleblower and reported her concerns about Bennett to senior management at Partou.During his trial it emerged parents had raised concerns to the nursery in the six months before he was caught.James said news of Bennett's conviction led him to worry about the worker's behaviour when he was an apprentice."I was concerned that he didn't become a predatory paedophile when he moved to the nursery in Bristol – I believe he was always a predatory paedophile," he said.James said CCTV in nurseries should be a "minimum requirement"."If I was to go through choosing a nursery again, it's something I'd need to have in place," he said.Another parent, Helen, said she wanted to see mandatory, actively monitored CCTV and stronger safeguards, including higher qualification requirements for staff and strict enforcement of two-person working."Mandatory CCTV should not be a problem – especially in places with extremely vulnerable people, where it's most needed," she said."Something positive needs to come out of such a horrendous thing," she added.Helen said the uncertainty of not knowing if anything could have happened had led her to "read into everything"."Any comments [from my child] about nursery now, you don't know how to interpret them."My child will sometimes start a conversation saying, 'mummy, I didn't tell you this thing that happened at nursery' and I start shaking every time she says it," she added.Katie and John Meehan, whose daughter Genevieve was killed at a nursery in Stockport in 2022, have also been campaigning for mandatory CCTV in nurseries.CCTV footage showed nursery worker Kate Roughley tightly swaddling nine-month-old Genevieve, strapping her to a beanbag and leaving her unattended. She died of asphyxiation.John Meehan said that - while CCTV was not a "silver bullet" - use of it could "identify unsafe practices" or provide evidence for the regulator and police when harm occurred."For parents entrusting their precious and vulnerable children to a nursery, the confidence and reassurance these safeguards can provide are vital," he said.The Department for Education said it had strengthened recruitment and safeguarding requirements at nurseries.It said this included full criminal record checks for staff working closely with children, checks on references before a hire, new safeguarding training and clear processes for staff to raise concerns.Allegations or concerns that a staff member has harmed a child or is unsuitable to work with children should be reported to the council's Local Authority Designated Officer (LADO).The nursery where Bennett was an apprentice said one concern was raised following Bennett's conviction, which the LADO confirmed did not meet the threshold for investigation.The nursery was rated Outstanding by Ofsted at the time of Bennett's employment. The regulator told the BBC there had been no concerns raised during Bennett's employment at the nursery.In an email sent to parents following Bennett's conviction, the nursery said Bennett was employed as an apprentice and subject to a high level of supervision.A man who worked at the nursery at the same time as Bennett said he had not noticed any suspicious behaviour but was concerned staff could sometimes be left to work alone, even if they had no previous childcare experience."I had never worked in early years or childcare before," he said."The chances of being alone when changing a nappy were quite high."The door wasn't always open when [Bennett] was changing nappies," he added.A member of staff who worked at the nursery after Bennett had left, said she had often felt overwhelmed with the number of children she was given to look after.While she said whistleblowing policies and safeguarding procedures were clearly explained at the nursery and people were encouraged to report anything that did not sit right, she added that complaints she raised about having too many children were not addressed, and she eventually quit her job."It was horrendously overwhelming and eventually I couldn't do it anymore," she said.Rachel said the impact of knowing her child went to a nursery where Bennett was working would be "lifelong"."The moment I found out he had been convicted confirmed how I had felt that year about Nathan Bennett," she said.And although she cannot do anything about the lack of CCTV at the Somerset nursery, she said mandatory video monitoring could deter other potential offenders - or provide proof for other families after a crime had happened."It didn't deter Nathan Bennett, but without it he would be free to continue committing these crimes," she said.

schema.headline: Parents live in fear paedophile nursery worker harmed their children

title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Florence Pugh attended the Governors Awards in Hollywood at the weekendByHelen BushbyCulture reporterFlorence
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Florence Pugh attended the Governors Awards in Hollywood at the weekendByHelen BushbyCulture reporterFlorence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery. The actress wrote on Instagram, external how stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend". "I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pugh has spoken out before about judgement about how women look Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds"."The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg."Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming". "I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again"."I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Pugh is no stranger to a striking red carpet outfit Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived"."Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance. "I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said. "But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.  'Please be gentle'Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs."I was... horrified," she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.The actress concluded by urging followers to think about their attitudes towards physical appearance."I understand that we are in a warped part of image history right now, with beauty standards changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with," she said. "But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance."I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us."It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye."

schema.headline: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation

title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
description: Figure caption, Who are the investors ready to jump on Anthropic?ByKali HaysTechnology reporterSamira HussainNorth America business correspondent and
body: Figure caption, Who are the investors ready to jump on Anthropic?ByKali HaysTechnology reporterSamira HussainNorth America business correspondent and Osmond ChiaBusiness reporterUpdated 1 hour agoAnthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62.bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world. A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares. Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately. The firm's $1.5tn valuation makes it more valuable than Walmart and Samsung and on almost on a par with Tesla and Meta.But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document. Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".Crucial test for AIIn total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years agoOpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years. However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.Rapid riseAnthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.OpenAI has voiced similar sentiments and delayed its plans to list on the stock market in order to address AI safety concerns. Image source, Getty ImagesTechnology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower."AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.Competition from low-cost rival models is growing. Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply. And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

schema.headline: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut

title: Leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByTarah WelshHousing correspondent and Jade Thompson Updated 2 hours agoThe government is to introduce new laws to scrap the
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByTarah WelshHousing correspondent and Jade Thompson Updated 2 hours agoThe government is to introduce new laws to scrap the ownership rules for flats in England and Wales and cap ground rents at £250 a year.Under the plans, which will not become law until at least next year, most new leasehold flats will eventually be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the 21st century".But the Residential Freehold Association says the plan is an "unprecedented abuse" of their rights, which will wipe billions from the value of pension funds, which have invested heavily in property.The Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, to be published on Thursday, is likely to contain further details on when the measures would come into force. In order to become law, the bill would first need to be approved by both Houses of Parliament, a process that will take several months. 'Continuous torture cell' The bill will also include plans to cap ground rent - the annual fee paid by current leaseholders to their freeholder - at £250 from 2028. That will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.  Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".Image source, Fozia MalikImage caption, Fozia Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat againWhen she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.Scotland does not have leasehold tenures, while Northern Ireland has just a handful of leasehold properties.The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other other countries around the world, which do not have leaseholds.It comes as more than 1,000 leaseholders have contacted the BBC over the past two years with complaints about the current system.Risk of two-tier system  Campaigners have welcomed many of the reforms, but questioned what happens to the millions of people who already own leasehold homes.While the legislation is expected to reshape ownership for new developments, converting existing leasehold buildings into commonhold is far more complicated. And it has led to concerns that current leaseholders will be left behind.Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier system of those buying new homes and existing leaseholders.He began campaigning on behalf of flat owners following the Grenfell Tower tragedy. He says: "It's so complicated, will the measures that are being introduced actually benefit everyone?"Image source, Giles GroverImage caption, Giles Grover, from the campaign group End Our Cladding Scandal, says there is a risk the proposed changes will create a two-tier systemThe government says the bill will make it easier for existing leaseholders to convert to commonhold, abolish forfeiture - so people cannot lose their homes over relatively small debts - improve transparency around service charges and crack down on estate charges.Pennycook says it will transform "the experience of homeownership for existing leaseholders by giving them greater rights and protections and providing them with easy and effective escape routes".However, the issue about how existing leaseholders can move into commonhold and how freeholders should be compensated remains unresolved.A spokesperson for the Residential Freehold Association, which represents the UK's largest freeholders, says £18.7bn "could be wiped out from investments overnight". The association says property investors, which often include pension funds, have invested £15bn in residential ground rents. Get in touchDo you own a leasehold property? Will the changes impact your property purchase or sale?

schema.headline: Leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales

title: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
description: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Gr
body: After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100, external - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype." But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN, external branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building. "The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote, external, but he added "there are also nits to pick".For The New York Times, external one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors. Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action. But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian, external describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics."They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".Writing for Forbes, external, Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".The Washington Post, external said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg, external's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review."It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it."While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m). The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.Additional reporting by Jasmine Sandhar

schema.headline: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece

title: Golf: LIV paid players millions as UK businesses owed thousands
description: UK firms owed thousands as Saudi-backed LIV paid golfers millionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy in SeptemberBy
body: UK firms owed thousands as Saudi-backed LIV paid golfers millionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy in SeptemberByTom GrundyBBC Sport senior journalistLIV Golf - backed by more than $5bn (£3.8bn) from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund - paid millions to players and executives in the weeks before filing for bankruptcy, while leaving a trail of unpaid bills from UK suppliers.BBC Sport has seen invoices from five small businesses totalling hundreds of thousands of pounds, all of which were overdue before LIV made its final payments to players.Global Infusion Group,, external a Buckinghamshire company that provided catering at July's LIV Golf UK event, is still owed £321,671, due on 7 August.Suffolk-based BD365 Clean, external provided 108 cleaning staff and is owed £75,225, most of which was due on 20 July and 13 August."It just feels completely immoral," said Bonnie May, chief executive of Global Infusion Group."It really matters to a business of our scale. The impact has been huge, both personally and professionally."Only $2m (£1.5m) has been earmarked so far by the Saudi owners to pay unsecured creditors, leaving many smaller companies unsure if they will receive anything at all.Yet court filings reveal LIV made 59 payments to golfers on 31 July, amounting to $16.6m (£12.6m) and matching prize money for the same LIV Golf UK event.A further $34.2m (£25.9m) went to players between 17 August and 3 September following tournaments in New York and Indianapolis, including $6.4m (£4.9m) to 2026 champion Jon Rahm just five days before the bankruptcy filing.Figure caption, LIV Golf's bankruptcy and its debt to British businesses'How can they sleep at night?'Four senior LIV executives also received retention bonuses totalling nearly $3m (£2.3m) in August."It's sickening," said Krissi Foskett, owner of BD365 Clean, who described the unpaid bills as "almost an extinction-level event" for her team."How can they sleep at night, knowing they are potentially putting companies out of business?"Meanwhile, public records list more than £3,000 owed to Goodysphere,, external a family-run Yorkshire firm that provides a sensory bus designed to help autistic children who may find busy events overwhelming.LIV Golf did not respond to our request for comment.However, in August, LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil said he hoped they would be able to pay their suppliers."What I would say to them is we're doing everything we can to make sure we can do right by them and the work they committed."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Players received a total of $16.6m (£12.6m) five days after the LIV Golf UK event'It's Saudi money, that’s safe as houses'The controversial breakaway league had been owned and bankrolled by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) since its launch season in 2022.But in April, the fund announced it would end its backing after the 2026 season, putting LIV's future in doubt."Our understanding was that the funding would take LIV through 2026," said Global Infusion Group's May, whose company had about 60 staff catering for players and broadcasters."We weren't aware the funding had already stopped and there wasn't enough to actually fulfil their obligations."PIF's multi-billion-dollar investment helped it to lure some of golf's biggest names and disrupt the PGA Tour's dominance of the sport."It's Saudi money, that's safe as houses, we thought," said Foskett."Their head honchos came along and enjoyed hospitality. We were there cleaning up at one o'clock in the morning then back in at five in the morning, only to be treated like this."PIF remains the majority owner of Newcastle United, while Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 Fifa World Cup."I'm sure the country won't want to be saddled with the characterisation that it doesn't pay its bills," said professor Simon Chadwick, who is an expert in the business and politics of sport across Africa, Europe and Asia."I do find it surprising that they would simply walk away. I think they would want to engage in some kind of remedial action, particularly in terms of managing their image and reputation."Image source, BD365 CleanImage caption, Krissi Foskett said her team "went the extra mile" and sifted through waste by hand to help LIV hit sustainability targetsFilmmaker Joe Bentley spent eight days from April working on a video for LIV's YouTube channel that is still online.He is owed nearly £6,000, with £2,226 due on 31 July.The video was part of the 'LIV Back' series, set up to "focus on the impact LIV players and teams are making off the course".He filmed at two schools taking part in 'Little Sticks', a LIV outreach programme which aimed to provide golf equipment and training in areas of deprivation."You feel massively deflated, a bit cheated and undervalued," said Bentley."Everyone I dealt with at LIV was lovely. The first email I sent chasing was to a production coordinator or a manager and even she was appalled that we hadn't been paid."Gateshead Council is also owed £1,912, due on 22 August, relating to 'Little Sticks'."Transformation is not a short-term process," said Professor Chadwick."If you're going to embark on investment programmes in community sport, grassroots sport, you've got to make a long-term commitment and those changes have got to take place."What happens next?LIV filed for bankruptcy protection in New Jersey on 8 September."The contacts we had sadly all lost their jobs," said Giles Mitchell, whose company, Office Pantry, supplied food to LIV's office on London's South Bank."We didn't hear anything from them and then their emails started bouncing back."There was hope the competition could survive in some form with new investment, but in November LIV announced it was winding down operations.In the bankruptcy filings, LIV estimated it had between $500m and $1bn (£380m-£760m) in liabilities and at least 1,000 creditors.The largest 30 unsecured creditors alone were listed with claims of more than $64m (£49m)."I think the message is loud and clear to somebody like me that, no, we're not going to get paid for any of this," said May."If anything did come our way, I'm thinking it's going to be pennies in the pound, nothing which will have any impact, or even cover our legal fees."Who else is owed money?Fourteen golfers were among the published creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims.Rahm topped the list with a claim of $7.5m (£5.7m), which he agreed to give up as part of his deal to leave the league.Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m/£4.3m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m/£4.2m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m/£3.6m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m/£2.6m) also featured.IMG Media, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, and British golf YouTuber Rick Shiels were each listed with claims of more than $1m (£760,000) too.Meanwhile, BBC Sport understands the R&A is owed about £500,000 for advice on sustainable maintenance of courses used by LIV.A hearing is scheduled for January to consider the wind-down plan, but creditors may have to wait longer to find out how much they will get back."I've had nights just sat there in tears, thinking, what is the point," said BD365 Clean's Foskett."How much comes in will honestly depend on whether or not the business will still be going at the end of January."I don't want to throw the towel in."

schema.headline: Golf: LIV paid players millions as UK businesses owed thousands

title: Lewis Hamilton: Ferrari driver says there are no trust issues between himself and team
description: Lewis Hamilton says there is "definitely not" a trust problem between him and his Ferrari team.The seven-time champion has twice in the past four race
body: Lewis Hamilton says there is "definitely not" a trust problem between him and his Ferrari team.The seven-time champion has twice in the past four races ignored a call to pit for fresh tyres, both times to his competitive disadvantage.The most recent time, in the Sao Paulo Grand Prix on 8 November, Hamilton stayed out on worn slick tyres in worsening rain and ended up spinning before pitting on the next lap.Before this weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, Hamilton spoke positively of his relationship with his race engineer Carlo Santi."We're constantly working on our communication," said Hamilton, who had a different race engineer last year."It's been a lot better this year. Carlos (sic) has done an amazing job. And those particular two times, particularly the last time, was just I didn't have the information I needed. I got the call right at the last minute."We'll just continue to work on the processes. We're super united in what's working, in the right direction."The previous time Hamilton ignored a call to pit was in Singapore, when he decided to stay out during a virtual safety car period. He later apologised. At the following race in Austin, he explained that he was "always looking at ways to win, always looking at doing potentially something different. And I wanted to be on a different strategy, not just the same strategy as Charles (Leclerc), where we just follow each other".Hamilton and Leclerc both insisted that relations between the pair were good after clear-the-air talks in Brazil following a disagreement at the previous race in Mexico, where a tangle on the first lap led to them throwing away a potential one-two and handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen. Hamilton said in Las Vegas on Wednesday: "Charles is a great driver. The detail we went into about stuff like that in terms of when we close the visor, it's very clear we understand each other."We understand each other's boundaries and the ultimate goal, which is to get the best result for the team."So I don't feel that that will be a problem going forward. I have no concerns or worries about racing him, and I don't think he does with me either."Leclerc said: "The discussion went very well. Very, very quickly, after a few sentences already, the tension that was there was not there anymore, and it was all fine."We both work in the direction of having that second place in the constructors' championship. The second place in the constructors' is important."It's also true that we've got a relatively big margin behind, which doesn't mean we need to minimise that, and we still have to work as a team. But what is really important for me now is to try and win before the end of the season and win the race."He added that "everything has been taken out of proportion" but he is "kind of used to it" have been at Ferrari since 2019. "Of course, the goal is not always to agree, and that will never happen," he added. "We can have different opinions, and that was the case, for example, in Mexico. But just the fact of speaking eased all tensions, and we were completely fine with it."It's not that we had to speak for an hour, even though it ended up lasting an hour, just because we had a good time and we started speaking about also many other things in trying to bring the team and to help the team go forward."But the discussion about the tension was like maybe five or 10 minutes, and then the air was clean, and that's it."

schema.headline: Lewis Hamilton: Ferrari driver says there are no trust issues between himself and team

title: Westside Cowboy named BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026
description: Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy
body: Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals. The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan. Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK, providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network. About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.

schema.headline: Westside Cowboy named BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026

title: Wales v Australia: Steve Tandy makes four changes to side that beat All Blacks
description: Exeter flanker Kane James is set to win his second cap from the bench after making his debut against Argentina in July.Scarlets centre or fly-half Joe
body: Exeter flanker Kane James is set to win his second cap from the bench after making his debut against Argentina in July.Scarlets centre or fly-half Joe Hawkins also comes in for Ospreys playmaker Dan Edwards, who suffered an ankle injury in training that has led to Cardiff's Jarrod Evans being called into the Nations Championship squad.Taine Plumtree will cover the second row in the absence of Beard, who suffered a shoulder injury against New Zealand.Number eight Taine Basham and wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb drop out of the matchday squad after starting against the All Blacks.Tandy says he had always intended to make changes."We made nearly 350 tackles, the ball in play time was one of the highest in Test rugby in the last three years and we have got competition," said the Wales head coach."The plan was always to freshen up and we are likely to do similar for the week after, because we need to find out about players."We have fresh and hungry players coming in, which will add the energy that we need at the weekend."The training environment is getting more competitive in certain positions we have the ability to put people in and feel confident about performance."Eleven players will have started all three Tests - eight from English clubs and the Scarlets trio of full-back Blair Murray, centre Eddie James and fly-half Sam Costelow.Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Adams; Costelow, T Williams; Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, Jenkins, Carter, Mann, Morgan, Wainwright.Replacements: Elias, G Thomas, Lewis, Plumtree, K James, Morgan-Williams, Hawkins, Hennessey.Australia: Wright; Jorgensen, Suaalii, Ikitau, Potter; Gorden, Lonergan; Kailea, Paenga-Amosa, Tupou, Canham, Hooper, Valetini, Tizzano, Wilson (capt).Replacements: Pollard, Bell, Alaalatoa, Williams, McReight, Thomas, Donaldson, Daugunu.Referee: Luc Ramos (France).Assistant referees: Karl Dickson (England) & Jeremy Rozier (France).TMO: Eric Gauzins (France).

title: Leandro Riedi: Tennis the saviour for player who tried to take own life
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Leandro Riedi reached the last 16 of the US Open men's singles in 2025ByBBC Sport tennis news reporterWarning
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Leandro Riedi reached the last 16 of the US Open men's singles in 2025ByBBC Sport tennis news reporterWarning: This article contains references to suicideThe clues were there. Leandro Riedi struggled to even force a smile after winning a match which moved him closer to the Wimbledon main draw.These are the moments usually cherished and celebrated by a player ranked outside of the world's top 100.The Swiss player's solemn reaction was jarring, but then nobody outside of his immediate circle knew what had happened a few days earlier.Shortly before Wimbledon qualifying began in June 2024, Riedi had tried to take his own life.Panic attacks had been plaguing the world number 137 for almost 18 months. Anxiety and self-doubt had been around for much longer.The toll they were taking on his mental health meant he felt there was no other way out."I always had anxiety. I was always a shy person, especially when I was younger. I always had this mindset that I wasn't good enough," Riedi told BBC Sport."I always thought I needed to do something special. I have to be perfect. This was my mental battle all the time."February 2023 to November 2024 was a horrible period of time. I was always scared of having a panic attack. I had no control over it whatsoever."Very few people knew the extent of Riedi's mental health issues until he revealed last week that he had attempted suicide.The 24-year-old wants to make two things clear.Firstly, he is not looking for sympathy. He has only decided to talk about his experience to "send a strong message" for others struggling with their mental health.Secondly, he is now in a "very good" place, thanks to professional treatment he has received over the past two years."I hope nobody ever has to go through what I did - it's horrifying and scary," Riedi said."But I want to be an example it can turn out well."The past - 'I don't know how I played at Wimbledon'Figure caption, I don't know how I played at Wimbledon - RiediIn his darkest moments Riedi found salvation in the sport which he started playing as a three-year-old growing up in Zurich."I felt really home at a tennis court - I was able to perform and I was able to play," he said."So tennis was my saviour in that time. It helped me to go out of my thoughts for one second and focus on doing what I love."It goes some way to explaining why Riedi decided to still compete at Wimbledon so soon after attempting to end his life.Looking back, he is unsure how he summoned the strength to play."My coach told me to go home. He was the only one who knew. But then what? Be sad at home?" Riedi said."I didn't want to go home. I wanted to stay and I wanted to play. It was a horrible, horrible week."After the first round I remember I just left and went to the hotel. Usually you're excited and happy about a win, but I couldn't speak."In his hotel room Riedi continued to have troubled thoughts.He credits his psychologist, who stayed awake with Riedi until 3am to make sure he was not alone, for saving his life.Riedi went on to win his second qualifying match before losing in the third and final round. At first he felt the pressure was "lifted", but not competing created a void.Riedi describes how he was "scared" to leave his hotel room for the next two weeks, only going out to collect food deliveries from the lobby.Tennis continued to be the only force which Riedi thought provided purpose. He managed to leave London for a tournament in Sweden, banking on it "bringing happiness".But, after winning a match in Gstaad, he started to realise that going on to court was merely a placebo effect.The catalyst of change came a few weeks later when a knee injury - the first "big injury" of his career - required surgery following the US Open."It was devastating for me because I knew my one happiness - tennis - was gone," Riedi said."In tennis I always had to fight [my mental health] because I was still playing. I didn't want to show any weakness."Then I realised I didn't want to fight any more. I wanted to help it. I wanted to work with it."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Riedi (right) reached the Surbiton Challenger final just before Wimbledon qualifying in 2024, finishing runner-up to South Africa's Lloyd Harris (left)The present - opening up to send 'strong message'Focusing on tennis and receiving the support of his "closest people" helped Riedi through his most troubled times.Reopening his psychological "wounds", and discussing his inner trauma with experts, has been the key to his recovery.He no longer has suicidal thoughts. The panic attacks have stopped. He still has anxiety but possesses the coping mechanisms to prevent it being debilitating.Riedi had been planning to open up publicly for several months. He still felt nervous when he hit publish on his social media post, but he has been heartened by an overwhelmingly warm response."I have got messages from all over the world. Someone texted me from India saying they saw the post and are going through something similar right now," Riedi said."They said 'Your message really helped me. It gave me some power to believe it's going to work.' That's exactly what I was aiming for."People think tennis pros have all they need. I wanted to showcase that it's OK not to be OK even though others think you have everything."Riedi says his mental health struggles were caused by "private issues" in his life and were not a consequence of his career.But, with players increasingly speaking out about mental burnout, he wants his words to drive further change.The ATP already provides an in-house psychology and wellbeing service, which offers confidential support at tournaments and remotely.If a mental health disorder prevents a player from competing for at least six months, they can apply for a protected ranking. It allows them to enter tournaments without penalty when they are ready to return.Riedi says the governing bodies can "never do too much", but he thinks there is still an issue on the men's tour with reaching out for support."For me, mental health is like a muscle. If your knee is injured, you do surgery and take care of it," he said."If you're injured in your mind, it's like you can't speak about it. That's not good."I hope my message shows tennis players, or anyone, that speaking out isn't a weakness. It's actually the opposite. It's strong and brave."The future - 'sky is the limit' after making peaceSince working on his mental health, Riedi has produced some of the best results of his career.He came through qualifying to reach the last 16 of the 2025 US Open - his standout performance at a Grand Slam tournament - and climbed to a career-high world ranking of 116 this year.The most poignant moment came in June 2025 when he returned to Wimbledon.A year on from his suicide attempt, Riedi decided to stay at the same Chelsea hotel because he wanted "make peace" with what had happened."It was very emotional, but in a good way," he said."I was like, 'wow, when you really work on something, if you stay consistent about something, one year can do so much'."This year Riedi's progress on the court has been hampered by a torn tendon in a wrist.Being sidelined for six months led to some friends wondering why he does not stop playing professionally. He says his "love and passion" for tennis will not allow him.Riedi says the "sky is still the limit" and plans to make his comeback at the start of 2027, using a protected injury ranking to enter Australian Open qualifying."I really had to go through big obstacles, but I'm very proud I did this at such a young age. I'm actually this guy who just likes life," he said."I love to do things. I want to be happy. I want to be excited for my future and not be scared."If you have been affected by issues raised in this article, there is information and support available on BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Leandro Riedi: Tennis the saviour for player who tried to take own life

title: BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026: Cast your vote
description: Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.Fans from the UK can
body: Voting is now open for the BBC Men's Footballer of the Year 2026 award, which will be presented at Sports Personality of the Year.Fans from the UK can vote from the five-player shortlist of Jude Bellingham, Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe, Rodri and Lamine Yamal.The vote closes on Friday, 27 November at 09:00 GMT.The winner of the award - new for this year - will be presented during the live Sports Personality of the Year show on Sunday, 13 December.Alex Kay-Jelski, Director of BBC Sport, said: "From the drama and excitement of the men's World Cup to the moments that have captivated fans across the domestic and international game, 2026 has given us so much to celebrate. "Our inaugural BBC Men's Footballer of the Year award is about recognising the players who have made this year so special, inspired fans and left their mark on the game. "It's a fantastic shortlist, and I can't wait to see who the public choose as our first-ever winner."The shortlist was selected by an expert panel comprising former international players and some of the BBC's most respected football voices, bringing together a wealth of experience and insight from across the game.The panel included Cesar Azpilicueta (Spain), Scott Brown (Scotland), Olivier Giroud (France), Shay Given (Republic of Ireland), Hassan Kachloul (Morocco), Lucas Leiva (Brazil), Benni McCarthy (South Africa), Alan Shearer, Ellen White (both England) and Ashley Williams (Wales).Read more on the five contenders and cast your vote below.

title: How Premier League's big six keep getting richer and richer
description: Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food ch
body: Companies put their money where supporters are prepared to spend it. It is a simple fact of business in every country, a reality of football's food chain.In England, Liverpool, Arsenal and Manchester United traditionally dominated viewing figures, column inches, shirt sales and sponsorship.Over the past 20 years they have been joined by Chelsea, Manchester City and Tottenham.This group of clubs now generate so much money it is hard to imagine how they can fail in the long term - even factoring in short-term performance issues.Let's look at how the gap has grown.We will use Everton, the only club not in the big six to be in the Premier League since its inception in 1992.This tells a tale of how even one of the league's founding members can be left trailing well behind.In 2009-10, the gap in revenues between the big-six average and Everton was £120m. In 2024-25, that gap had grown to £442m.So what has driven this huge escalation?In large part it is the boom in international TV rights.Kieran Maguire, professor of football finance at the University of Liverpool, told BBC Sport that it has attracted companies prepared to pay large sums to be associated with the Premier League's top clubs."The big football brand clubs have global fanbases and that makes them very attractive to global commercial partners, especially for sponsorship and front-of-shirt deals," Maguire said."You combine that with the fact that the Premier League is broadcast to 190 different countries around the world, and especially the international audiences - that allows the clubs to negotiate very good prices."Only 10% of Everton's revenue comes from commercial deals, while for the big six it is 45%.It means Everton, and other clubs in the league, are heavily reliant on broadcast income. It makes up 66% of their revenue.For Everton at least, this should change following the move to Hill Dickinson Stadium.But that is unlikely to be enough to stop the gap increasing.It has taken a few years, but Aston Villa and Newcastle have begun to increase their revenue.This is largely thanks to the financial rewards of Champions League football. But even Uefa has created a system which entrenches the position of the biggest clubs.When the European Super League plan was torpedoed, Uefa created a new financial deal called the value pillar.This reserves 35% of all Champions League revenues, or £713m, for the historically most successful clubs.At the end of the league phase last season City are estimated to have earned £37.9m from the value pillar, Liverpool £35.5m and Chelsea £33.3m. Newcastle received only £13.6m.The good news for Villa is their coefficient has improved greatly, aided by last season's Europa League win.Their value pillar is projected to be worth £25m this season. But that will still be less than the big six clubs in the competition.The cards are stacked against an ambitious club - not just domestically, but in Europe too.Take a look at the financial trend of the big six and one thing becomes noticeable - Chelsea are beginning to fall behind.In the past two seasons, and for the first time in recent history, the Blues recorded the lowest revenues of the big six.Not just by a small amount. They were £74m behind Tottenham, and £200m below Liverpool and Manchester City.City's matchday income is the lowest, with the club's huge revenues largely due to commercial deals. City, however, have been found guilty of breaching the Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18, inflating the value by using "sham contracts" with sponsors. The club deny wrongdoing and have lodged an appealed against the verdict.Chelsea's problem is simple - seats.Stamford Bridge has a capacity of only 40,000, with no easy scope for expansion. The rest of the big six have grounds which hold at least 60,000.Chelsea generated an average spend per fan of £80 in 2024-25, the second highest in the league after Arsenal.Yet with 20,000 fewer tickets sold than their big six rivals, Chelsea's total matchday revenues are dwarfed."Matchday spend has become increasingly important," Maguire said. "There has been a flatlining of broadcast revenues, especially since 2017."As a consequence, clubs have had to look at alternative methods of increasing revenues, especially with costs both on the pitch and off pitch rising so fast."Matchday revenue has effectively stalled for Chelsea, rising only £16m over the past 10 years. United's has grown by £69m and Spurs, thanks to their new ground, by £85m."Chelsea are far more reliant upon player sales," Maguire said. "There is a growing divide because the global appeal is very much aligned with three or four clubs. "Arsenal have re-established themselves with their progress in the Champions League. Manchester United are a brand in their own right. And Liverpool have expanded Anfield from 44,000 to 61,000, with many of those extra seats having gone to commercial."Chelsea's successful player trading model has so far limited the impact.But there are signs that, financially at least, the big six could become the big five.You might recall that Villa and Newcastle were not fans of the old profit and sustainability rules (PSR).PSR forced both clubs to sell some of their best players to balance the books.That has changed this season with squad-cost ratio (SCR).There is a key difference with SCR, in that it allows a club to spend the money they generate on players. PSR limited losses so was more restrictive."This does make it a little easier for the likes of Villa and Newcastle to spend money," Maguire said. "But it is still heavily weighted in favour of the big six."SCR is different to PSR rather than better. For some people, change is advantageous. For others, it isn't."So what does this mean?  The big six generate hundreds of millions of pounds more than the other clubs. So they can spend hundreds of millions of pounds more on their squads.This makes the big six even more powerful in the transfer market. "Look at the clubs who voted against SCR - Brighton, Brentford, Bournemouth, Crystal Palace, Fulham and Leeds," Maguire said."It's very noticeable that those clubs have traditionally been very good at player sales, while they have tended to have lower matchday and commercial revenues."Most of the big six  - the outlier being Chelsea - are not remotely close to the Premier League's 85% SCR limit.If you give clubs more money to spend on transfers, the likelihood is they will do just that. And the numbers back that up.Look at this summer.Premier League clubs spent £3.5bn - not only a highest total for a summer window, but it almost smashed the record for a whole season, the £3.53bn set in 2025-26. The annual accounting cost of previous transfers, or amortisation, has been rising year on year."Over the course of the last decade, transfer amortisation has more than doubled and close to tripled," Maguire said."Which means that on average, clubs in the Premier League are now spending, or now have a cost which goes into their SCR calculations of just under £100m."Uefa fears that SCR will make matters worse, and have an inflationary impact across Europe.And you can see why it is concerned.In the summer 13 Premier League clubs broke their transfer record.Brentford, Brighton, Palace, Leeds and Nottingham Forest all spent more than £40m on a player - unthinkable until recently.So we have learned that the big six have more money than ever, and the gap is so huge it is impossible for any other club to compete with them, financially at least.And this is an important point: other than Villa and Newcastle, the other clubs are not trying to compete with the big six.Clubs like Brentford and Brighton have shown that smart models are just as effective as fat wallets.They sign the potential stars of the future, nurture them and then sell them to the big six.Football's ecosystem recycles the big-six money through the transfer market.But it is a precarious business for these other clubs."The smaller clubs have to get it right on a more regular basis than the bigger clubs," Maguire said."The big six can afford to make signings which are £60m and £70m, who turn out to be relative flops, and still have those players on high wages for several years."And this is perhaps the key point about the vast finances of the big six.The commercial power of the big six does not guarantee success. After all, United sit in the relegation zone.Yet Mauricio Pochettino, their new manager, may well get the chance to revamp the squad despite the club spending £945m on players in the past five years.The richest clubs can try to spend their way out of trouble. Again and again.But the rest of the league are only a couple of bad transfer windows from catastrophe.And that is the real gap between the big six and the rest.

schema.headline: How Premier League's big six keep getting richer and richer
